title: Reinforcement Learning with Pytensor
text:
Preface
This book is a hands-on companion to Sutton & Barto’s Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction. Chapter by chapter, we take the algorithms from the book — bandits, dynamic programming, temporal-difference learning, and beyond — and implement them from scratch in Python using PyTensor.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Pytensor
text:
Why PyTensor?
Most reinforcement learning tutorials reach for plain NumPy loops or a deep learning framework. PyTensor sits in an interesting middle ground: you describe the agent–environment interaction symbolically — as a computation graph — then compile it once and run it fast. This turns out to be a natural fit for reinforcement learning:

Shared variables hold the agent’s mutable state, such as value estimates and visit counts.
Updates express the book’s “increment toward the target” learning rules directly, as declarative state transitions applied on every step.
Vectorization lets us run thousands of independent experiments in parallel — one compiled step advances them all at once, with no Python loops.

Along the way, the symbolic style forces us to be explicit about what the agent knows, what it observes, and how its beliefs change.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Pytensor
text:
Who this book is for
The reader we have in mind has some Python and probability background and is working through (or has read) Sutton & Barto. This book is not a replacement for theirs: we state the key ideas and equations, but the emphasis here is on turning them into working, testable code and reproducing the classic figures and experiments.

title: Bandit Algorithms
text:
The \(k\)-armed bandit problem
A hands-on companion to Chapter 2 of Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction.
We implement and compare three classic strategies for the multi-armed bandit problem:
At each time step \(t\) you choose one of \(k\) actions \(A_t \in \{0,\dots,k-1\}\) and receive a reward \(R_t\) drawn from a fixed-but-unknown distribution that depends only on the action you picked. The true value of an action is its expected reward,
\[q_*(a) \;=\; \mathbb{E}[R_t \mid A_t = a].\]
If you knew \(q_*\) you would always pull \(\arg\max_a q_*(a)\). However, You don’t, so you must estimate it from experience while you act. That is the exploration vs. exploitation trade-off: pull the arm that looks best now (exploit), or pull a less-certain arm to learn more about it (explore)?
We track an estimate \(Q_t(a) \approx q_*(a)\). The workhorse is the sample-average / incremental update: after observing reward \(R_t\) for the chosen action \(A_t = a\),
\[
N_{t+1}(a) = N_t(a) + 1
\]
\[
\qquad Q_{t+1}(a) = Q_t(a) + \frac{1}{N_{t+1}(a)}\bigl(R_t - Q_t(a)\bigr).
\]
Read it as NewEstimate = OldEstimate + StepSize · (Target − OldEstimate)
This is what we encode as a PyTensor update. Our implementation will vectorize across the 2000 independent runs of the testbed. Instead of 2000 Python loops, every shared variable has shape (n_runs, k) and one compiled step() advances all runs at once.

title: Bandit Algorithms
text:
The 10-armed testbed
To compare algorithms fairly we use S&B’s testbed setup:

\(k = 10\) arms.
For each independent run, the true values \(q_*(a)\) are drawn once from \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\).
A reward for pulling arm \(a\) is then \(R_t \sim \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(q_*(a),\, 1\bigr)\).
We average performance over 2000 runs to get smooth learning curves.

We generate \(q_*\) in NumPy and let the agent’s perception of the environment, selecting an arm, sampling its noisy reward, and updating beliefs live inside the compiled PyTensor graph.

title: Bandit Algorithms
text:
ε-greedy
The simplest balance of exploration and exploitation:
\[
A_t = \begin{cases}\arg\max_a Q_t(a) & \text{with probability } 1-\varepsilon \quad(\textbf{exploit})\\[2pt]
\text{a uniformly random arm} & \text{with probability } \varepsilon \quad(\textbf{explore}).\end{cases}
\]
After acting we apply the incremental sample-average update.
Two things worth explaining about PyTensor mechanics :








Mechanic
What it does
Why it matters




Threading the RNG
The random generator is a shared variable holding immutable state, so a random op can’t mutate it in place. Instead each op takes the current state and returns a pair: new_state, sample. To draw three times in one step we chain the states rng → rng1 → rng2 → rng3 and then hand the final state back with updates={rng: rng3, ...}.
That write is what makes the next step() call continue the stream instead of replaying the same “random” numbers.


Vectorized (advanced) indexing
rows is [0, 1, ..., N_RUNS-1] and a is a length N_RUNS vector holding the arm each run chose. Pairing them, Q[rows, a] picks exactly one entry per run: run 0’s chosen arm, run 1’s chosen arm, and so on.
Q[rows, a] reads all 2000 runs’ current estimates at once, and set_subtensor(Q[rows, a], q_new) writes all 2000 updates at once, with no Python loop over runs.




def _shared_state(n_runs: int, k: int):
    Q = pytensor.shared(np.zeros((n_runs, k), floatX), name="Q") # value estimates
    N = pytensor.shared(np.zeros((n_runs, k), floatX), name="N") # visit counts
    q_star = pytensor.shared(np.zeros((n_runs, k), floatX), name="q*") # true values
    return Q, N, q_star


def build_epsilon_greedy(n_runs: int, k: int, epsilon: float, seed: int=0):
    rng = pt.random.shared_rng(np.random.default_rng(seed))
    Q, N, q_star = _shared_state(n_runs, k)
    rows = pt.arange(n_runs)

    # action selection: explore with prob epsilon
    rng1, uni_samples = rng.uniform(size=(n_runs,))
    explore = uni_samples < epsilon
    rng2, rand_a = rng1.integers(0, k, size=(n_runs,))
    greedy_a = pt.argmax(Q, axis=1)
    a = pt.where(explore, rand_a, greedy_a)

    # environment: reward ~ N(q_*(a), 1)
    rng3, noise = rng2.normal(size=(n_runs,))
    reward = q_star[rows, a] + noise

    # incremental sample-average update
    n_new = N[rows, a] + 1.0
    q_old = Q[rows, a]
    q_new = q_old + (reward - q_old) / n_new
    N_upd = pt.set_subtensor(N[rows, a], n_new)
    Q_upd = pt.set_subtensor(Q[rows, a], q_new)

    optimal = pt.eq(a, pt.argmax(q_star, axis=1))  # did we pick the best arm?
    step = pytensor.function(
        [],
        [reward, optimal],
        updates={rng: rng3, N: N_upd, Q: Q_upd}
    )
    return SimpleNamespace(step=step, Q=Q, N=N, q_star=q_star)

title: Bandit Algorithms
text:
Upper-Confidence-Bound (UCB)
ε-greedy explores indiscriminately. UCB instead explores purposefully, preferring arms that are either promising or under-explored. It selects
\[
A_t = \arg\max_a \left[\, Q_t(a) + c\,\sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{N_t(a)}}\, \right]
\]
The square-root term is a confidence radius: it shrinks as an arm is sampled more (\(N_t(a)\uparrow\)) and slowly grows for arms left untouched (\(\ln t\uparrow\)). The constant \(c>0\) tunes how aggressively we explore. Any arm with \(N_t(a)=0\) is treated as having an infinite bonus, so UCB tries every arm once before getting selective.

def build_ucb(n_runs: int, k: int, c: float, seed: int=0):
    rng = pt.random.shared_rng(np.random.default_rng(seed))
    Q, N, q_star = _shared_state(n_runs, k)
    t = pytensor.shared(np.array(1.0, floatX), name="t")  # global time step
    rows = pt.arange(n_runs)

    # Unvisited arms (N==0) get an infinite bonus so they are tried first.
    bonus = pt.where(pt.eq(N, 0.0), np.inf, c * pt.sqrt(pt.log(t) / pt.maximum(N, 1e-12)))
    a = pt.argmax(Q + bonus, axis=1)

    rng1, noise = rng.normal(size=(n_runs,))
    reward = q_star[rows, a] + noise

    n_new = N[rows, a] + 1.0
    q_old = Q[rows, a]
    q_new = q_old + (reward - q_old) / n_new
    N_upd = pt.set_subtensor(N[rows, a], n_new)
    Q_upd = pt.set_subtensor(Q[rows, a], q_new)

    optimal = pt.eq(a, pt.argmax(q_star, axis=1))
    step = pytensor.function(
        [],
        [reward, optimal],
        updates={rng: rng1, N: N_upd, Q: Q_upd, t: t + 1.0}
    )
    return SimpleNamespace(step=step, Q=Q, N=N, q_star=q_star, t=t)

title: Bandit Algorithms
text:
Thompson sampling
A Bayesian strategy: maintain a posterior distribution over each arm’s unknown value and, each step, sample one value per arm and act greedily on the samples. Arms we’re uncertain about have wide posteriors, so they occasionally produce a high sample and get explored — exploration falls out of the probability matching automatically, with no ε or \(c\) to tune.
For our Gaussian testbed (rewards have known variance 1) we use a conjugate Gaussian model with a standard-normal prior on each arm’s mean, \(\mu_a \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\). After observing \(n\) rewards for an arm with running sum \(S\), the posterior is Gaussian with
\[
\text{mean} = \frac{S}{1+n}, \qquad \text{variance} = \frac{1}{1+n}
\]






Tip



The \(1+n\) comes from adding the prior precision \(1\) to the data precision \(n\).


We sample \(\theta_a \sim \mathcal{N}(\text{mean}, \text{variance})\) for every arm and pull \(\arg\max_a \theta_a\). Here the sufficient statistics are the per-arm reward sum and count rather than a running mean.

def build_thompson(n_runs: int, k: int, seed: int=0):
    rng = pt.random.shared_rng(np.random.default_rng(seed))
    sumR = pytensor.shared(np.zeros((n_runs, k), floatX), name="sumR") # running reward sum per arm
    N = pytensor.shared(np.zeros((n_runs, k), floatX), name="N") # visit counts
    q_star = pytensor.shared(np.zeros((n_runs, k), floatX), name="q*")
    rows = pt.arange(n_runs)

    # Conjugate Gaussian posterior (prior N(0,1), known reward variance 1).
    post_mean = sumR / (1.0 + N)
    post_var = 1.0 / (1.0 + N)
    rng1, z = rng.normal(size=(n_runs, k))
    theta = post_mean + pt.sqrt(post_var) * z # one posterior sample per arm
    a = pt.argmax(theta, axis=1)

    rng2, noise = rng1.normal(size=(n_runs,))
    reward = q_star[rows, a] + noise

    sumR_upd = pt.set_subtensor(sumR[rows, a], sumR[rows, a] + reward)
    N_upd = pt.set_subtensor(N[rows, a], N[rows, a] + 1.0)

    optimal = pt.eq(a, pt.argmax(q_star, axis=1))
    step = pytensor.function([], [reward, optimal],
                             updates={rng: rng2, sumR: sumR_upd, N: N_upd})
    return SimpleNamespace(step=step, sumR=sumR, N=N, q_star=q_star)

title: Bandit Algorithms
text:
Running the experiments
reset reinitializes an agent’s shared state and initializes a fresh set of true values.
run_experiment then calls the compiled step() for N_STEPS, recording at each step the average reward across the 2000 runs and the fraction of runs that picked the optimal arm.

def reset(agent, q_star_values):
    n_runs, k = q_star_values.shape
    agent.q_star.set_value(q_star_values)
    agent.N.set_value(np.zeros((n_runs, k), floatX))
    if hasattr(agent, "Q"):
        agent.Q.set_value(np.zeros((n_runs, k), floatX))
    if hasattr(agent, "sumR"):
        agent.sumR.set_value(np.zeros((n_runs, k), floatX))
    if hasattr(agent, "t"):
        agent.t.set_value(np.array(1.0, floatX))


def run_experiment(agent, q_star_values, n_steps):
    reset(agent, q_star_values)
    avg_reward = np.empty(n_steps)
    pct_optimal = np.empty(n_steps)
    for tstep in range(n_steps): # This can be a pytensor scan
        r, opt = agent.step() # one vectorized step across all runs
        avg_reward[tstep] = r.mean()
        pct_optimal[tstep] = opt.mean()
    return avg_reward, pct_optimal


q_star = make_testbed(N_RUNS, K, seed=42)

agents = {
    "ε=0 (greedy)": build_epsilon_greedy(N_RUNS, K, 0.0,  seed=1),
    "ε=0.01": build_epsilon_greedy(N_RUNS, K, 0.01, seed=1),
    "ε=0.1": build_epsilon_greedy(N_RUNS, K, 0.1,  seed=1),
    "UCB (c=2)": build_ucb(N_RUNS, K, 2.0, seed=1),
    "Thompson": build_thompson(N_RUNS, K, seed=1),
}

results = {}
for name, agent in agents.items():
    results[name] = run_experiment(agent, q_star, N_STEPS)

The results are summarized below.







Algorithm
Behavior on this testbed




Greedy (\(\varepsilon=0\))
Climbs fastest at first, then plateaus low: it fixates on whatever looked good early and never discovers better arms.


\(\mathbf{\varepsilon=0.1}\)
Learns quickly but its 10% forced exploration caps it (it can’t exceed ~91% optimal once it knows the best arm since it still explores).


\(\mathbf{\varepsilon=0.01}\)
Learns slower but overtakes \(\varepsilon=0.1\) eventually (not shown in figure due to limited number of N_STEPS).


UCB
Typically beats ε-greedy on this testbed: its exploration is targeted, and the early spike comes from trying each arm once.


Thompson sampling
Usually the strongest and needs no exploration hyperparameter.

title: Finite Markov Decision Processes
text:
The running example: the Recycling Robot
A hands-on companion to Chapter 3 of Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction.
A guided, worked-example tour of the core objects of reinforcement learning:
We build everything symbolically with PyTensor so the equations in the markdown map almost one-to-one onto the code.
A mobile robot collects soda cans. It decides whether to actively search, wait for someone to bring a can, or recharge its battery. Its battery is either high or low.
A finite MDP is the tuple \(\langle \mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, p, r, \gamma\rangle\):

recycling robot




\(\mathcal{S}\)
states
{high, low}


\(\mathcal{A}\)
actions
{search, wait, recharge} (recharge only in low)

transition probabilities
battery dynamics below


\(r(s,a,s')\)
reward on a transition

\(\gamma\in[0,1)\)

how much we value the future




Dynamics
Searching from high keeps the battery high with probability \(\alpha\). Searching from low keeps it low with probability \(\beta\), and with probability \(1-\beta\) the battery dies and the robot must be rescued — it is carried back to a charger (state becomes high) with a big penalty of \(-3\). Searching yields expected reward \(r_\text{search}\), waiting yields \(r_\text{wait}\) (\(r_\text{search} > r_\text{wait}\)), and recharging yields \(0\).


Transition graph
The full MDP as an interactive graph, rendered with gravis. Circles are states, boxes are (state, action) pairs. Edges connect a state to its available actions; each arrow out of an action node is labeled with its transition probability and reward (using \(\alpha=0.9\), \(\beta=0.7\), \(r_\text{search}=2\), \(r_\text{wait}=1\)).

title: Finite Markov Decision Processes
text:
Define the MDP as tensors
We index states = [high, low] and actions = [search, wait, recharge].
The whole MDP lives in two 3-D arrays:

\(P[s,a,s'] = p(s'\mid s,a)\) with shape (|S|, |A|, |S'|) = (2, 3, 2)
\(R[s,a,s'] = r(s,a,s')\) with the same shape

Because recharge is not available in high, we keep a boolean availability mask avail[s,a]. So that \(P\) stays a valid probability distribution everywhere, we let the unavailable (high, recharge) entry be a harmless self-loop; the mask makes sure no policy or max ever uses it.
We pick concrete numbers: \(\alpha=0.9\), \(\beta=0.7\), \(r_\text{search}=2\), \(r_\text{wait}=1\), \(\gamma=0.9\).

# index helpers
HIGH, LOW = 0, 1
SEARCH, WAIT, RECHARGE = 0, 1, 2
state_names  = ["high", "low"]
action_names = ["search", "wait", "recharge"]
nS, nA = 2, 3

# parameters
alpha = 0.9
beta = 0.7
r_search = 2.0
r_wait = 1.0
gamma_val = 0.9

# transition tensor P[s, a, s']
P = np.zeros((nS, nA, nS))
P[HIGH, SEARCH, HIGH] = alpha
P[HIGH, SEARCH, LOW] = 1 - alpha
P[LOW, SEARCH, HIGH] = 1 - beta
P[LOW, SEARCH, LOW] = beta
P[HIGH, WAIT, HIGH] = 1.0
P[LOW, WAIT, LOW]  = 1.0
P[LOW, RECHARGE, HIGH] = 1.0
P[HIGH, RECHARGE, HIGH] = 1.0 # unavailable -> harmless self-loop (masked out)

# reward tensor R[s, a, s']
R = np.zeros((nS, nA, nS))
R[HIGH, SEARCH, HIGH] = r_search
R[HIGH, SEARCH, LOW] = r_search
R[LOW, SEARCH, HIGH] = -3.0 # rescued
R[LOW, SEARCH, LOW] = r_search
R[HIGH, WAIT, HIGH] = r_wait
R[LOW, WAIT, LOW]  = r_wait
# recharge rewards are 0 already

# availability mask avail[s, a]
avail = np.array([[1, 1, 0], # high: search, wait, recharge zeroed out
                  [1, 1, 1]], # low:  search, wait, recharge
                 dtype=bool)

assert np.allclose(P.sum(axis=2), 1.0), "each P[s,a,:] must sum to 1"
print("P sums over s' (should be all 1s):\n", P.sum(axis=2))

P sums over s' (should be all 1s):
 [[1. 1. 1.]
 [1. 1. 1.]]



Expected immediate reward \(r(s,a)\)
It’s often handier to work with the reward expected over the next state:
\[ r(s,a) \;=\; \mathbb{E}[R_{t+1}\mid S_t=s, A_t=a] \;=\; \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\, r(s,a,s'). \]
In PyTensor this is just an elementwise product summed over the last axis.

# Convert into PyTensor constants, and make gamma a symbolic scalar so we can plug in different discounts
P_t   = pt.as_tensor_variable(P) # (2, 3, 2)
R_t   = pt.as_tensor_variable(R) # same shape
avail_t = pt.as_tensor_variable(avail.astype("float64")) # (2, 3)
gamma = pt.scalar("gamma")

# r(s, a) = sum_s' P[s,a,s'] * R[s,a,s']
r_sa = (P_t * R_t).sum(axis=2) # (2, 3)

print("Expected immediate reward r(s,a):")
print(r_sa.eval())

[[2.  1.  0. ]
 [0.5 1.  0. ]]

title: Finite Markov Decision Processes
text:
Rewards and returns
The agent’s goal is to maximize the return; the discounted sum of future rewards. For a trajectory starting at time \(t\),
\[
G_t \;=\; R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \cdots \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k R_{t+k+1}
\]
Two equivalent ways to read this:

Flat sum: weight the \(k\)-th future reward by \(\gamma^k\).
Recursively: the seed of every Bellman equation: \[
G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\,G_{t+1}
\]

Let’s compute \(G_0\) for a concrete reward sequence two ways and check that they agree.

# A sample reward sequence R_1, R_2, ..., R_T  (as if we rolled out an episode)
rewards = np.array([2.0, 2.0, -3.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0]) # This could correspond to search -> search -> rescue ...
r_seq = pt.vector("r_seq")

# method 1: flat discounted sum, G_0 = sum_k gamma^k * R_{k+1}
k = pt.arange(r_seq.shape[0])
G0_flat = (gamma ** k * r_seq).sum()

# method 2: recursive G_t = R_{t+1} + gamma G_{t+1}, via scan
# scan from the LAST reward backwards, carrying the running return.
def back_step(r_t, G_next, g):
    return r_t + g * G_next

returns_rev = pytensor.scan(
    fn=back_step,
    sequences=[r_seq[::-1]], # walk rewards in reverse
    outputs_info=pt.zeros(()), # G_{T+1} = 0
    non_sequences=[gamma],
    return_updates=False
)
G_all = returns_rev[::-1] # G_0, G_1, ..., G_{T-1}
G0_rec = G_all[0] # Since it is backwards the first is the last

f = pytensor.function(inputs=[r_seq, gamma], outputs=[G0_flat, G0_rec, G_all])
g0a, g0b, gall = f(rewards, gamma_val)
print(f"G_0 (flat sum)  = {g0a:.4f}")
print(f"G_0 (recursive) = {g0b:.4f}")
print("Return G_t from every step t:", gall)

G_0 (flat sum)  = 3.2071
G_0 (recursive) = 3.2071
Return G_t from every step t: [ 3.20708  1.3412  -0.732    2.52     2.8      2.     ]



Why discount? Because it changes decisions.
Discounting isn’t about the rewards themselves; the robot always receives them in full when they arrive. It’s about how the agent ranks futures when choosing what to do now. Suppose the robot is in low and weighs two possible futures:

search now (impulsive): grab cans immediately (+2, +2), the battery dies (−3, rescued to high), then keep searching → \(R = [2, 2, -3, 2, 2, 2]\)
recharge first (patient): forgo any reward this step (0), then search safely from high → \(R = [0, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2]\)

The sequences only differ in steps 0 and 2, so \(G_0^{\text{search}} - G_0^{\text{recharge}} = 2 - 5\gamma^2\), which changes sign at \(\gamma^* = \sqrt{2/5} \approx 0.63\):

\(\gamma < 0.63\): myopic - the immediate +2 dominates and the crash barely registers leads to search now.
\(\gamma > 0.63\): far-sighted - the −3 crash and the bigger tail count leads to recharge first.







Note



\(\gamma<1\) also guarantees the infinite sum converges, which is what makes the value functions below well-defined.


Drag the slider across 0.63 and watch the verdict in the title flip. This previews an upcoming section where at \(\gamma=0.9\) the optimal policy in low is recharge.

text:
Policies
A policy \(\pi(a\mid s)\) is a distribution over actions in each state. We store it as a matrix pi[s, a] whose rows sum to 1. To respect the action constraints we put zero probability on unavailable actions.
We start with the uniform random policy (pick uniformly among the available actions in each state).

pi = np.where(avail, 1.0, 0.0)
pi = pi / pi.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) # normalize each row
print("Uniform random policy pi[s, a]:")
for s in range(nS):
    probs = {action_names[a]: round(pi[s, a].item(), 3) for a in range(nA) if avail[s, a]}
    print(f"  {state_names[s]:>4}: {probs}")

pi_t = pt.as_tensor_variable(pi) # (2, 3)

Uniform random policy pi[s, a]:
  high: {'search': 0.5, 'wait': 0.5}
   low: {'search': 0.333, 'wait': 0.333, 'recharge': 0.333}



Collapsing the MDP under a fixed policy
Once the policy is fixed, the MDP becomes a plain Markov reward process. Averaging the dynamics over actions gives a state-to-state transition matrix and a per-state reward:
\[
P^\pi_{s s'} = \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\, p(s'\mid s,a), \qquad r^\pi_s = \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\, r(s,a).
\]

# P_pi[s, s'] = sum_a pi[s,a] P[s,a,s'] -> (2, 2)
P_pi = (pi_t[:, :, None] * P_t).sum(axis=1) # Sum over actions
# r_pi[s]    = sum_a pi[s,a] r(s,a) -> (2,)
r_pi = (pi_t * r_sa).sum(axis=1)

print("P_pi (state-to-state transitions under uniform policy):\n", P_pi.eval())
print("r_pi (expected reward per state):", r_pi.eval())

section: The state-value function \(v_\pi\) - Bellman expectation equation
text:
The state-value function \(v_\pi\) - Bellman expectation equation
\(v_\pi(s)\) is the expected return when starting in state \(s\) and following policy \(\pi\):
\[
v_\pi(s) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid S_t = s].
\]
Using \(G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}\) and averaging over actions and next states gives the Bellman expectation equation:
\[
v_\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a\mid s) \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r(s,a,s') + \gamma\, v_\pi(s')\big].
\]
In the collapsed MRP form this is linear in \(v_\pi\):
\[
\mathbf{v}_\pi = \mathbf{r}^\pi + \gamma\, P^\pi \mathbf{v}_\pi.
\]

Method A - solve it exactly
Rearranging to, \((I - \gamma P^\pi)\,\mathbf{v}_\pi = \mathbf{r}^\pi\), gives a small linear system we can solve directly.

I = pt.eye(nS)
v_closed = pt.linalg.solve(I - gamma * P_pi, r_pi)

v_closed_val = v_closed.eval({gamma: gamma_val})
print("v_pi (exact linear solve):")
for s in range(nS):

Treat the Bellman equation as an update rule and iterate it. The map:

def eval_step(v_prev, r_pi, P_pi, g):

    return_updates=False

title: Finite Markov Decision Processes
text:
The action-value function \(q_\pi\)
\(q_\pi(s,a)\) is the expected return from taking action \(a\) in state \(s\) and then following \(\pi\):
\[
q_\pi(s,a) = \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r(s,a,s') + \gamma\, v_\pi(s')\big].
\]
Two consistency relations tie \(v_\pi\) and \(q_\pi\) together:
\[
q_\pi(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\, v_\pi(s'),
\qquad
v_\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\, q_\pi(s,a).
\]
We compute \(q_\pi\) from the \(v_\pi\) we just found, then verify the second relation.

v = v_closed # reuse the exact v_pi
# q_pi[s, a] = sum_s' P[s,a,s'] (R[s,a,s'] + gamma v[s'])
q_pi = (P_t * (R_t + gamma * v[None, None, :])).sum(axis=2) # (2, 3)

q_val = q_pi.eval({gamma: gamma_val})

print("        " + "  ".join(f"{a:>9}" for a in action_names))
for s in range(nS):

    print(f"  {state_names[s]:>4}: " + "  ".join(cells_))

# Check v_pi(s) == sum_a pi(a|s) q_pi(s,a)
v_from_q = (pi_t * q_pi).sum(axis=1)
print("\nv_pi from q_pi:", v_from_q.eval({gamma: gamma_val}))

title: Finite Markov Decision Processes
text:
Optimality - the Bellman optimality equations
We don’t just want to evaluate a policy, we want the best one. The optimal value function satisfies the Bellman optimality equation:






Note



note the max, not an average over \(\pi\)


\[
v_*(s) = \max_{a} \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r(s,a,s') + \gamma\, v_*(s')\big].
\]
This is still a contraction, so value iteration, repeatedly applying the right-hand side, converges to \(v_*\). The only change from policy evaluation is swapping the policy-average for a max over available actions (we mask the unavailable ones with \(-\infty\) so they’re never chosen).

NEG = -1e9 # stand-in for -infinity on unavailable actions

def vi_step(v_prev, P_t, R_t, avail_t, g):
    # q[s,a] = sum_s' P (R + g v')
    q = (P_t * (R_t + g * v_prev[None, None, :])).sum(axis=2) # (2, 3)
    q = pt.where(avail_t > 0, q, NEG) # mask unavailable
    return q.max(axis=1) # max over actions

v_star_seq = pytensor.scan(
    fn=vi_step,
    outputs_info=pt.zeros((nS,)),
    non_sequences=[P_t, R_t, avail_t, gamma],
    n_steps=200,
    return_updates=False
)
v_star = v_star_seq[-1]

v_star_val = v_star.eval({gamma: gamma_val})
print("v_*(s):")
for s in range(nS):
    print(f"  v_*({state_names[s]:>4}) = {v_star_val[s]:.4f}")

v_*(s):
  v_*(high) = 18.3486
  v_*( low) = 16.5138



Extracting the optimal policy and \(q_*\)
Given \(v_*\), the optimal action in each state is the greedy one:
\[
\pi_*(s) = \arg\max_a\; q_*(s,a),
\qquad
q_*(s,a) = \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r(s,a,s') + \gamma\, v_*(s')\big].
\]

q_star = (P_t * (R_t + gamma * v_star[None, None, :])).sum(axis=2) # (2, 3)
q_star_masked = pt.where(avail_t > 0, q_star, NEG)
greedy = q_star_masked.argmax(axis=1) # (2,)

q_star_val = q_star.eval({gamma: gamma_val})
greedy_val = greedy.eval({gamma: gamma_val})

print("Optimal policy pi_*:")
for s in range(nS):
    print(f"  in {state_names[s]:>4}: {action_names[int(greedy_val[s])]}")

print("\nq_*(s, a):")
print("        " + "  ".join(f"{a:>9}" for a in action_names))
for s in range(nS):
    cells_ = [f"{q_star_val[s,a]:9.4f}" if avail[s,a] else f"{'  NULL':>9}" for a in range(nA)]
    print(f"  {state_names[s]:>4}: " + "  ".join(cells_))

title: Dynamic Programming
text:
Gridworld
A hands-on companion to Chapter 4 of Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction.
In the previous chapter we defined \(v_\pi\), \(q_\pi\) and the Bellman equations; now we turn them into algorithms that compute optimal policies when we have a perfect model \(p(s'\mid s,a)\) of the environment.
We work through the dynamic programming toolkit, building each piece symbolically in PyTensor:
Everything below is one of these two one-line operators applied over and over:
\[
\underbrace{v(s)\leftarrow \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r + \gamma v(s')\big]}_{\textbf{expectation backup (evaluation)}}
\qquad
\underbrace{v(s)\leftarrow \max_a \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r + \gamma v(s')\big]}_{\textbf{optimality backup (value iteration)}}
\]
Both are \(\gamma\)-contractions, which is why iterating them converges.
As an example we will use the Gridworld example, introduced in the chapter as the following:
A \(4\times4\) grid of 16 states. The two shaded corners, the top-left (state 0) and bottom-right (state 15), are terminal. From any non-terminal state the four actions up, down, left, right move deterministically one cell; an action that would step off the grid leaves the agent where it is.
Every transition earns a reward of \(-1\) until the terminal state is reached, so the task is undiscounted (\(\gamma = 1\)) and episodic; the agent wants to escape to a corner in as few steps as possible. Terminal states are absorbing with value pinned to \(0\).
As in the previous chapter the whole MDP lives in two arrays \(P[s,a,s']=p(s'\mid s,a)\) and \(R[s,a,s']=r(s,a,s')\), here both deterministic.

title: Dynamic Programming
text:
Policy evaluation
Given a fixed policy \(\pi\), policy evaluation computes its value function \(v_\pi\) by turning the Bellman expectation equation into an update rule and iterating it to its fixed point:
\[
v_{k+1}(s) \;=\; \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r(s,a,s') + \gamma\, v_k(s')\big].
\]
Collapsing the policy into a Markov reward process this linear map
\[
\mathbf v \mapsto \mathbf r^\pi + \gamma P^\pi \mathbf v
\]
is a \(\gamma\)-contraction. We run it with pytensor.scan, masking terminal states back to \(0\) each sweep.
We evaluate the equiprobable random policy \(\pi(a\mid s)=\tfrac14\).

pi_t = pt.matrix("pi") # (16, 4)

r_pi = (pi_t * r_sa).sum(axis=1) # (16,)

def eval_step(v_prev, r_pi, P_pi, g, mask):
    return mask * (r_pi + g * pt.dot(P_pi, v_prev)) # mask pins terminals to 0

v_eval_seq = pytensor.scan(
    fn=eval_step,
    outputs_info=pt.zeros((nS,)), # v_0 = 0
    non_sequences=[r_pi, P_pi, gamma, nonterminal], # nonterminal is our mask in eval_step
    n_steps=600,
    return_updates=False
)
v_eval = v_eval_seq[-1]
eval_fn = pytensor.function([pi_t, gamma], v_eval)

pi_random = np.ones((nS, nA)) / nA
v_random  = eval_fn(pi_random, 1.0)
show_grid(v_random, "v_pi for the equiprobable random policy:")

title: Dynamic Programming
text:
Policy improvement
Now that we can score a policy, how do we get a better one?
For each state, look one step ahead with the value we just computed and ask which action looks best:
\[
q_\pi(s,a) = \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r(s,a,s') + \gamma\, v_\pi(s')\big],
\qquad \pi'(s) = \arg\max_a q_\pi(s,a).
\]
The policy improvement theorem guarantees \(v_{\pi'} \ge v_\pi\) for every state, with strict improvement somewhere unless \(\pi\) was already optimal. Acting greedily can never make things worse.
Below we make one greedy policy from the random-policy values. Even this single step turns the aimless random walk into something that clearly heads for the corners.

v_sym = pt.vector("v")
q_sa  = (P_t * (R_t + gamma * v_sym[None, None, :])).sum(axis=2) # (16, 4)
greedy_sym = q_sa.argmax(axis=1)
q_fn = pytensor.function([v_sym, gamma], [q_sa, greedy_sym])

def greedy_policy(v_val, g):
    "Deterministic greedy policy (as a one-hot matrix) and its action ids."
    _, a_star = q_fn(v_val, g)
    pi_new = np.zeros((nS, nA))
    pi_new[np.arange(nS), a_star] = 1.0
    return pi_new, a_star

title: Dynamic Programming
text:
Policy iteration
Policy iteration simply alternates the two steps until the greedy policy stops changing:
\[
\pi_0 \xrightarrow{\text{eval}} v_{\pi_0} \xrightarrow{\text{improve}} \pi_1
\xrightarrow{\text{eval}} v_{\pi_1} \xrightarrow{\text{improve}} \cdots
\xrightarrow{} \pi_* .
\]
Because there are finitely many deterministic policies and each round strictly improves (or we stop), it converges to an optimal policy in a handful of iterations. On this gridworld the random policy already points roughly the right way, so it lands on \(\pi_*\) almost immediately.

pi = np.ones((nS, nA)) / nA  # start from the random policy
for it in range(50):
    v_val = eval_fn(pi, 1.0) # evaluation (to convergence)
    pi_new, a_ids = greedy_policy(v_val, 1.0) # improvement (greedy)

    if np.array_equal(pi_new, pi):
        print(f"policy stable after {it} improvement step(s)")
        break
    pi = pi_new

v_star_pi = eval_fn(pi, 1.0)
show_policy(a_ids, "Optimal policy pi_* (shortest path to a terminal state):")
show_grid(v_star_pi, "\nOptimal value v_* (negative distance to nearest corner):")

text:
Value iteration
Policy iteration runs evaluation to convergence inside every step - often overkill. Value iteration truncates evaluation to a single sweep and folds the improvement straight into it by using the Bellman optimality backup (a max instead of the policy average):
\[
v_{k+1}(s) = \max_a \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\big[r(s,a,s') + \gamma\, v_k(s')\big].
\]
It is the same max-backup we used for the recycling robot. On the gridworld it reaches \(v_*\) in just a few sweeps - the longest shortest-path is 6 moves, and information propagates one cell per sweep.

def vi_step(v_prev, P_t, R_t, g, mask):
    q = (P_t * (R_t + g * v_prev[None, None, :])).sum(axis=2) # (16, 4)
    return mask * q.max(axis=1)

v_vi_seq = pytensor.scan(
    fn=vi_step,
    outputs_info=pt.zeros((nS,)),
    non_sequences=[P_t, R_t, gamma, nonterminal],
    n_steps=100,
    return_updates=False
)

# how many sweeps until the value stops moving?
all_v = v_vi_seq.eval({gamma: 1.0}) # Just a single scan no outer loop
deltas = np.abs(np.diff(all_v, axis=0)).max(axis=1)
converged = int(np.argmax(deltas < 1e-9)) + 1
print(f"value iteration converged in {converged} sweeps")
show_grid(all_v[-1], "v_* from value iteration:")

text:
A richer test: the Gambler’s Problem
The gridworld is so easy that policy iteration finishes in one step.
The Gambler’s Problem has a far more interesting optimal value/policy, and is the classic showcase for value iteration.
A gambler bets on coin flips.

State: current capital \(s \in \{0,\dots,100\}\)
action: the stake/bet \(a \in \{0,1,\dots,\min(s,\,100-s)\}\)

On each flip the coin comes up heads with probability \(p_h\). Heads adds the stake to the gambler’s capital, tails loses it. The episode ends at \(\$0\) (lose) or \(\$100\) (win); the reward is \(0\) everywhere except \(+1\) on reaching \(\$100\). Undiscounted, \(\gamma = 1\).
We use \(p_h = 0.4\) an unfair coin, so in the long run we expect to lose money.






Note



The cap on the stake is due to having no benefit to exceeding $100.



ph_val = 0.4
GOAL = 100
nS_g = GOAL + 1
stakes = np.arange(0, GOAL // 2 + 1) # possible stakes 0 through 50

S = np.arange(nS_g)[:, None] # (101, 1) capital
A = stakes[None, :] # (1, 51) stake
win_idx = np.clip(S + A, 0, GOAL) # next capital on heads
lose_idx = np.clip(S - A, 0, GOAL) # next capital on tails
valid = (A >= 1) & (A <= np.minimum(S, GOAL - S)) # non-zero stakes

win_t = pt.as_tensor_variable(win_idx)
lose_t = pt.as_tensor_variable(lose_idx)
valid_t = pt.as_tensor_variable(valid.astype("float64"))
ph = pt.scalar("ph")

is_term = (np.arange(nS_g) == 0) | (np.arange(nS_g) == GOAL) # terminal states are $0 and $100

V_term = np.zeros(nS_g)
V_term[GOAL] = 1.0  # All values 0 except when capital is $100
V_term_t = pt.as_tensor_variable(V_term)
NEG = -1e9

def gambler_vi(V_prev, win, lose, valid, ph_, Vterm, tmask):
    q = ph_ * V_prev[win] + (1.0 - ph_) * V_prev[lose] # (101, 51)
    q = pt.where(valid > 0, q, NEG) # mask illegal stakes
    Vmax = q.max(axis=1)
    return tmask * Vterm + (1.0 - tmask) * Vmax # keep terminals pinned

    fn=gambler_vi,
    outputs_info=V_term_t, # start with terminals set
    non_sequences=[win_t, lose_t, valid_t, ph, V_term_t, term_mask],
    n_steps=500,
    return_updates=False

opt_stake[is_term] = 0

title: Dynamic Programming
text:
Asynchronous DP
The methods above do synchronous (Jacobi) sweeps where we compute every \(v_{k+1}(s)\) from the old \(v_k\), using two copies of the array.
Asynchronous DP updates states in place, one at a time, in any order, reusing the freshest values immediately. As long as every state keeps getting visited it still converges, and it often needs fewer updates because new information propagates within a sweep instead of waiting for the next one.
Here is the in-place (Gauss-Seidel) version of value iteration where we use an inner scan over states that uses set_subtensor to assign each new value back into the same vector, so a state updated early in the sweep is already visible to states updated later.

def inplace_state_update(s, V, P_t, R_t, g, mask):
    q_s = (P_t[s] * (R_t[s] + g * V[None, :])).sum(axis=1) # (nA,)
    new_val = mask[s] * q_s.max()
    return pt.set_subtensor(V[s], new_val) # write back in place

def inplace_sweep(V_in, P_t, R_t, g, mask):
    V_seq = pytensor.scan(
        fn=inplace_state_update,
        sequences=[pt.arange(nS)],
        outputs_info=V_in,
        non_sequences=[P_t, R_t, g, mask],
        return_updates=False
    )
    return V_seq[-1]

V_in = pt.vector("V_in")
one_sweep = pytensor.function([V_in, gamma], inplace_sweep(V_in, P_t, R_t, gamma, nonterminal))

V = np.zeros(nS)
for sweeps in range(1, 200):
    V_next = one_sweep(V, 1.0)
    if np.max(np.abs(V_next - V)) < 1e-9:
        break
    V = V_next
print(f"in-place (Gauss-Seidel) value iteration: {sweeps - 1} sweeps")
print(f"synchronous (Jacobi) value iteration: {converged} sweeps")

show_grid(V_next, "v_* from in-place value iteration:")

title: Dynamic Programming
text:
Generalized Policy Iteration (GPI)
Step back and notice everything we built is the same dance between two processes:

evaluation drives \(v\) toward \(v_\pi\) (make the value consistent with the policy),
improvement drives \(\pi\) toward greedy(\(v\)) (make the policy consistent with the value).

GPI is the umbrella term for letting these two interact at any granularity:



how many evaluation sweeps per improvement?
algorithm




infinite (evaluate to convergence)
policy iteration


exactly \(1\)
value iteration


some \(k\) in between
truncated policy iteration


in place / arbitrary order
asynchronous DP



They all chase the same fixed point - the single \((v_*, \pi_*)\) where both consistency conditions hold at once.

title: Dynamic Programming
text:
Recap
We implemented the chapter material on top of the same PyTensor MDP machinery from the previous notebook:

policy evaluation: iterate the expectation backup to \(v_\pi\)
policy improvement: greedy step, justified by the improvement theorem
policy iteration: alternate the two to \(\pi_*\)
value iteration: one-sweep evaluation via the optimality max-backup
asynchronous DP: in-place Gauss-Seidel updates, same fixed point in (theoretically) fewer sweeps
GPI: the unifying frame; every method above is one knob setting of “eval sweeps per improvement”

title: Monte Carlo Methods
text:
Utilities & Environment Setup
A hands-on companion to Chapter 5 of Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction.
Monte Carlo (MC) methods learn value functions and optimal policies from sampled episodes alone - not requiring a model. These samples are sequences \(S_0, A_0, R_1, S_1, A_1, R_2, \dots, S_T\) generated by interacting with an environment. The value of a state is estimated by:
\[
v_\pi(s) \;=\; \mathbb E_\pi\!\left[G_t \mid S_t = s\right]
\;\approx\; \text{average of the returns observed after visiting } s .
\]
Monte Carlo methods do not bootstrap. Meaning each estimate stands on complete returns, not on other previously computed estimates, and the cost of estimating one state is independent of the number of states.
We work through the following chapter topics:

title: Monte Carlo Methods
section: Why the gridworld again (and not Blackjack)?
text:
Why the gridworld again (and not Blackjack)?
The book’s running example is Blackjack, chosen because its dynamics are hard to write down but easy to sample. We instead reuse the \(4\times4\) gridworld from the Dynamic Programming chapter for the opposite reason: we already have its exact \(v_\pi\), \(q_\pi\) and \(v_*\), so every Monte Carlo estimate below can be checked against the truth. The MC agent never sees \(P\) or \(R\) - the model lives only inside the simulator it interacts with.

import warnings

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", UserWarning)  # gravis' pkg_resources import
    import gravis as gv

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
import pytensor
import pytensor.tensor as pt
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.io as pio

title: Monte Carlo Methods
section: The environment, and its exact answers
text:
The environment, and its exact answers
We use the same \(4\times4\) gridworld: terminal corners 0 and 15, four deterministic moves, \(-1\) per step until termination, undiscounted (\(\gamma=1\)). We rebuild the tensors \(P[s,a,s']\) and \(R[s,a,s']\), but from here on they play two very different roles:

the simulator uses them to generate experience (this is “the environment”), and
the DP oracle uses them to compute exact values we compare MC against.

The Monte Carlo algorithms themselves touch neither - they only ever see \((S_t, A_t, R_{t+1})\) triples.
We start with the grid’s fixed facts: sixteen states, four actions, the two absorbing corners, and the action codes we will print as arrows.

n_states, n_actions = 16, 4
TERMINAL_STATES = [0, 15]
terminal = np.zeros(n_states, dtype=bool)
terminal[TERMINAL_STATES] = True
UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT = 0, 1, 2, 3
ARROWS = {UP: "^", DOWN: "v", LEFT: "<", RIGHT: ">"}

Three plain-Python helpers: grid_step is the deterministic dynamics we are about to bake into \(P\), while show_grid and show_policy print a length-16 vector as a \(4\times4\) block so we can eyeball values and greedy actions as we go.

def grid_step(s, a):
    "Where action a takes you from state s (clamped to the grid, terminals absorb)."
    if s in TERMINAL_STATES:
        return s
    row, col = divmod(s, 4)
    if a == UP: row = max(row - 1, 0)
    elif a == DOWN: row = min(row + 1, 3)
    elif a == LEFT: col = max(col - 1, 0)
    elif a == RIGHT: col = min(col + 1, 3)
    return row * 4 + col

def show_grid(values, title=""):
    if title: print(title)
    for row in np.asarray(values, dtype=float).reshape(4, 4):
        print("  " + "  ".join(f"{x:6.1f}" for x in row))

def show_policy(actions, title=""):
    if title: print(title)
    chars = [ARROWS[int(a)] if not terminal[s] else "T"
             for s, a in enumerate(actions)]
    for row in range(4):
        print("   " + "  ".join(chars[row * 4:(row + 1) * 4]))

Filling \(P\) and \(R\) is one pass over every \((s, a)\) pair. The moves are deterministic, so exactly one entry of \(P[s,a,\cdot]\) is \(1\), and every step taken out of a non-terminal state earns \(-1\).

P = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions, n_states)) # p(s' | s, a)
reward_table = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions, n_states)) # r(s, a, s')
for s in range(n_states):
    for a in range(n_actions):
        s_next = grid_step(s, a)
        P[s, a, s_next] = 1.0
        if s not in TERMINAL_STATES:
            reward_table[s, a, s_next] = -1.0

The same arrays again as PyTensor constants, together with the expected one-step reward \(r(s,a) = \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\, r(s,a,s')\) and a symbolic \(\gamma\). Both the oracle and the simulator are built out of these.

P_sym = pt.as_tensor_variable(P)
reward_sym = pt.as_tensor_variable(reward_table)
not_terminal = pt.as_tensor_variable((~terminal).astype("float64"))
reward_mean = (P_sym * reward_sym).sum(axis=2) # r(s, a), the expected one-step reward
gamma_sym = pt.scalar("gamma")

The oracle is the policy-evaluation scan from the Dynamic Programming chapter: 600 sweeps of the expectation backup drive any policy’s \(v_\pi\) to convergence. A second compiled function turns a state-value vector into action values with one lookahead through the model, which is how we get \(q_\pi\).

# the DP oracle: exact v_pi and q_pi for any policy
pi_eval_sym = pt.matrix("pi")
P_pi = (pi_eval_sym[:, :, None] * P_sym).sum(axis=1) # p(s' | s) under pi
reward_pi = (pi_eval_sym * reward_mean).sum(axis=1)  # r(s) under pi

def evaluation_step(v_prev, reward_pi, P_pi, gamma, not_terminal):
    return not_terminal * (reward_pi + gamma * pt.dot(P_pi, v_prev))

v_eval = pytensor.scan(
    fn=evaluation_step,
    outputs_info=pt.zeros((n_states,)),
    non_sequences=[reward_pi, P_pi, gamma_sym, not_terminal],
    n_steps=600,
    return_updates=False,
)
evaluate_policy = pytensor.function([pi_eval_sym, gamma_sym], v_eval[-1])

v_sym = pt.vector("v")
action_values_of = pytensor.function(
    [v_sym, gamma_sym],
    (P_sym * (reward_sym + gamma_sym * v_sym[None, None, :])).sum(axis=2)
)

Policy improvement, also unchanged from the DP chapter: score every action by one-step lookahead and put all of the probability mass on the best one.

def greedy_from_values(v, gamma):
    "the greedy policy of a state-value vector, via one-step lookahead through the model"
    a_greedy = action_values_of(v, gamma).argmax(axis=1)
    pi_greedy = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    pi_greedy[np.arange(n_states), a_greedy] = 1.0
    return pi_greedy, a_greedy

Running the oracle on the equiprobable random policy at \(\gamma = 1\) gives the two prediction references, \(v_\pi\) and \(q_\pi\), with the terminal rows pinned to zero.

# exact answers we will test against
GAMMA = 1.0
pi_random = np.ones((n_states, n_actions)) / n_actions
v_pi_random = evaluate_policy(pi_random, GAMMA)
q_pi_random = action_values_of(v_pi_random, GAMMA)
q_pi_random[terminal] = 0.0
pi_star = pi_random

Policy iteration - alternating evaluation and greedification until the policy stops changing - gives the control references \(v_*\) and \(q_*\). Printing both value functions fixes the targets everything below has to converge to.

for _ in range(50): # policy iteration
    pi_new, a_star = greedy_from_values(evaluate_policy(pi_star, GAMMA), GAMMA)
    if np.array_equal(pi_new, pi_star):
        break
    pi_star = pi_new
v_star = evaluate_policy(pi_star, GAMMA)
q_star = action_values_of(v_star, GAMMA)
q_star[terminal] = 0.0

show_grid(v_pi_random, "exact v_pi (equiprobable random policy):")
print()
show_grid(v_star, "exact v_* :")

   -14.0   -18.0   -20.0   -20.0
   -20.0   -20.0   -18.0   -14.0
   -22.0   -20.0   -14.0     0.0

exact v_* :
     0.0    -1.0    -2.0    -3.0
    -1.0    -2.0    -3.0    -2.0
    -2.0    -3.0    -2.0    -1.0
    -3.0    -2.0    -1.0     0.0

title: Monte Carlo Methods
section: Simulating episodes with scan and a threaded RNG
text:
Simulating episodes with scan and a threaded RNG
Everything below consumes batches of episodes, so we build one compiled simulator that rolls out \(B\) episodes in parallel: the recurrent state of the scan is a length-\(B\) vector of current states, and each step samples \(A_t \sim \pi(\cdot\mid S_t)\) and \(S_{t+1} \sim p(\cdot\mid S_t, A_t)\) with batched categorical draws.
Two PyTensor mechanics are worth calling out:








Mechanic
What it does
Why it matters




RNG threading
In PyTensor’s random API every draw consumes an RNG state and returns a fresh one: rng, a = rng.categorical(p=...). Inside scan we make the RNG one of the recurrent outputs, so scan hands back the final RNG state, which we register in updates=.
That write is what makes consecutive calls of the compiled function continue the stream instead of replaying it.


Fixed-length padding
scan wants a fixed number of steps, but episodes end at random times. The terminal states are absorbing with reward 0, so we just keep “playing” after termination.
The padded steps add nothing to any return, and we mask them out of the statistics with not_terminal.



The rollout gives aligned tensors \(S, A, R\) of shape \((T, B)\) where row \(t\) holds the triple \((S_t, A_t, R_{t+1})\). Returns come from one more backwards scan, \(G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\, G_{t+1}\), and sample averages from a scatter-add (inc_subtensor, which accumulates over repeated indices).

rng_simulate = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=2026, name="rng_simulate")
pi_rollout_sym = pt.matrix("pi")   # policy to roll out, (n_states, n_actions)
s_start_sym = pt.lvector("s0")     # (n_episodes,) start states
a_start_sym = pt.lvector("a0")     # (n_episodes,) forced first actions (for exploring starts)
max_steps_sym = pt.iscalar("T")    # episode length cap

def simulate_step(s, rng, pi, P):
    rng, a = rng.categorical(p=pi[s]) # A_t ~ pi(.|S_t), batched over episodes
    rng, s_next = rng.categorical(p=P[s, a]) # S_{t+1} ~ p(.|S_t,A_t)
    return s_next, rng, a, reward_mean[s, a]

S_next_sym, rng_final, A_sym, R_sym = pytensor.scan(
    fn=simulate_step,
    outputs_info=[s_start_sym, rng_simulate, None, None],
    non_sequences=[pi_rollout_sym, P_sym],
    n_steps=max_steps_sym,
    return_updates=False,
)
S_sym = pt.concatenate([s_start_sym[None, :], S_next_sym[:-1]], axis=0)  # row t = S_t
simulate = pytensor.function(
    [pi_rollout_sym, s_start_sym, max_steps_sym],
    [S_sym, A_sym, R_sym],
    updates={rng_simulate: rng_final}
)

Monte Carlo with exploring starts needs every episode to begin at a chosen \((S_0, A_0)\) pair, so we draw that first transition outside the scan and hand the resulting state in as the scan’s initial value. After the forced pair the rollout is the ordinary one, so simulate_step is reused verbatim.

# exploring-starts variant: the first (state, action) pair is forced
rng_exploring_starts = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=99, name="rng_exploring_starts")
rng_after_start, s_first_sym = rng_exploring_starts.categorical(p=P_sym[s_start_sym, a_start_sym])
r_first_sym = reward_mean[s_start_sym, a_start_sym]

# after the forced first pair the rollout is the ordinary one, so `simulate_step` is reused
S_next_es_sym, rng_es_final, A_es_rest_sym, R_es_rest_sym = pytensor.scan(
    fn=simulate_step,
    outputs_info=[s_first_sym, rng_after_start, None, None],
    non_sequences=[pi_rollout_sym, P_sym],
    n_steps=max_steps_sym - 1,
    return_updates=False,
)

S_es_sym = pt.concatenate([s_start_sym[None, :], s_first_sym[None, :], S_next_es_sym[:-1]], axis=0)
A_es_sym = pt.concatenate([a_start_sym[None, :], A_es_rest_sym], axis=0)
R_es_sym = pt.concatenate([r_first_sym[None, :], R_es_rest_sym], axis=0)

simulate_exploring_starts = pytensor.function(
    [pi_rollout_sym, s_start_sym, a_start_sym, max_steps_sym],
    [S_es_sym, A_es_sym, R_es_sym],
    updates={rng_exploring_starts: rng_es_final}
)

The returns come from a second scan over the same \((T, B)\) reward block, run backwards so each \(G_t\) can reuse the \(G_{t+1}\) computed one step earlier. It is compiled once and applied to whole batches of episodes.

# discounted returns G_t = R_{t+1} + gamma * G_{t+1}, right to left
rewards_sym = pt.matrix("rewards")

def accumulate_return(r, G_next, gamma):
    return r + gamma * G_next

G_reversed = pytensor.scan(
    fn=accumulate_return,
    sequences=[rewards_sym],
    outputs_info=pt.zeros_like(rewards_sym[0]),
    non_sequences=[gamma_sym],
    go_backwards=True,
    return_updates=False,
)
returns_fn = pytensor.function([rewards_sym, gamma_sym], G_reversed[::-1])

Averaging sampled returns means summing them into buckets - one per state, or one per state-action pair - and dividing by how many landed there. inc_subtensor accumulates over repeated indices, so a single call gives both the weighted sums and the counts; the weights argument stays open for the importance-sampling ratios later on.

# scatter-add sample returns into buckets (states, or state-action pairs)
def make_aggregator(n_buckets):
    ids = pt.lvector("ids")
    values = pt.dvector("values")
    weights = pt.dvector("weights")
    sums = pt.inc_subtensor(pt.zeros((n_buckets,))[ids], weights * values)
    counts = pt.inc_subtensor(pt.zeros((n_buckets,))[ids], weights)
    return pytensor.function([ids, values, weights], [sums, counts])

aggregate_states = make_aggregator(n_states)
aggregate_state_actions = make_aggregator(n_states * n_actions)

The last ingredient separates first-visit from every-visit MC: a forward sweep through time that marks the earliest occurrence of each id within its episode. Passing this mask as the weights gives first-visit estimates; passing all ones gives every-visit.

def first_visit_mask(ids, n_buckets):
    "ids: (max_steps, n_episodes). True where an id appears for the first time in its episode."
    max_steps, n_episodes = ids.shape
    seen = np.zeros((n_episodes, n_buckets), dtype=bool)
    is_first_visit = np.zeros(ids.shape, dtype=bool)
    episodes = np.arange(n_episodes)
    for t in range(max_steps):
        is_first_visit[t] = ~seen[episodes, ids[t]]
        seen[episodes, ids[t]] = True
    return is_first_visit

section: Sample Averages Under a Moving Policy
text:
Sample Averages Under a Moving Policy
The textbook algorithm averages all returns ever collected for each pair. But during control the policy keeps changing, so old returns are samples of the wrong (much worse) policy. Pairs that the greedy policy stops visiting only receive a thin \(\varepsilon\)-trickle of new data, and their poisoned averages can misrank actions for a very long time.
\[
\underbrace{
    \left(1 - \varepsilon + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal A|}\right)}_{\text{greedy}
} +
\underbrace{(|\mathcal A| - 1)\cdot\tfrac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal A|}}_{\text{other actions}} = 1
\]
This \(\frac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal A|}\) floor on every action is exactly what makes the policy ε-soft: no action’s probability ever drops to zero, which guarantees continual exploration and lets the MC control convergence argument go through.

EPS = 0.1

def eps_greedy(Q, eps):
    "the eps-greedy policy of a Q table, as an (n_states, n_actions) matrix"
    pi = np.full((n_states, n_actions), eps / n_actions)
    pi[np.arange(n_states), Q.argmax(axis=1)] += 1 - eps
    return pi

def sample_average_trial():
    "eps-greedy MC control with Q = average of ALL returns ever seen."
    Q_sum, Q_count = np.zeros(n_states * n_actions), np.zeros(n_states * n_actions)
    Q = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    for iteration in range(300):
        pi_soft = eps_greedy(Q, EPS)
        s_start_iter = np_rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(~terminal), size=50).astype("int64")
        S_iter, A_iter, R_iter = simulate(pi_soft, s_start_iter, 50)
        G_iter = returns_fn(R_iter, GAMMA)
        SA_iter = S_iter * n_actions + A_iter
        first_visits_iter = first_visit_mask(SA_iter, n_states * n_actions) & ~terminal[S_iter]

        sums, counts = aggregate_state_actions(
            SA_iter[first_visits_iter].astype("int64"),
            G_iter[first_visits_iter],
            np.ones(first_visits_iter.sum())
        )

        Q_sum += sums
        Q_count += counts
        Q = np.where(Q_count > 0, Q_sum / np.maximum(Q_count, 1), 0.0).reshape(n_states, n_actions)
    a_greedy = Q.argmax(axis=1)
    pi_greedy = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    pi_greedy[np.arange(n_states), a_greedy] = 1.0
    return (np.abs(evaluate_policy(pi_greedy, GAMMA) - v_star).max(), Q, Q_count.reshape(n_states, n_actions), a_greedy)

We run five trials, then open up the worst one. If its greedy policy is wrong somewhere, we print the full \(Q\) row of the offending state alongside how many returns each action was averaged from.

trials = [sample_average_trial() for _ in range(5)]
value_gaps = [gap for gap, *_ in trials]
print("value gap to v* per trial: " + "   ".join(f"{gap:.1f}" for gap in value_gaps))

worst_trial = trials[int(np.argmax(value_gaps))]
if worst_trial[0] > 1e-9:
    worst_gap, Q_worst, Q_count_worst, a_worst = worst_trial
    stuck_state = int(np.abs(evaluate_policy(np.eye(n_actions)[a_worst], 1.0) - v_star).argmax())
    action_names = ["up", "down", "left", "right"]

    print(f"\nworst trial is stuck at state {stuck_state} "
          f"(greedy pick: {action_names[a_worst[stuck_state]]}):")

    for a in range(n_actions):
        print(f"   {action_names[a]:>6}: Q = {Q_worst[stuck_state, a]:.2f}"
              f" from {int(Q_count_worst[stuck_state, a])} returns")
else:
    print("(all five trials happened to converge this time - rerun to see one get stuck)")

the rarely-explored optimal action still averages in early garbage returns at an eps-trickle of new data it would need thousands more episodes to recover. The cure is to replace the sample average with a constant step size,
\[
Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha\,\big[G_t - Q(S_t, A_t)\big],
\]
an exponential recency-weighted average that forgets returns generated by long-dead policies. With forgetting, the same \(\varepsilon\)-greedy loop lands on the optimal greedy policy reliably:

ALPHA = 0.05
Q_soft = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))

soft_returns = []
for iteration in range(1000):
    pi_soft = eps_greedy(Q_soft, EPS)
    s_start_iter = np_rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(~terminal), size=50).astype("int64")
    S_iter, A_iter, R_iter = simulate(pi_soft, s_start_iter, 50)
    G_iter = returns_fn(R_iter, GAMMA)
    soft_returns.append(G_iter[0].mean())
    SA_iter = S_iter * n_actions + A_iter
    first_visits_iter = first_visit_mask(SA_iter, n_states * n_actions) & ~terminal[S_iter]

    sums, counts = aggregate_state_actions(
        SA_iter[first_visits_iter].astype("int64"),
        G_iter[first_visits_iter],
        np.ones(first_visits_iter.sum())
    )

    counts = counts.reshape(n_states, n_actions)
    batch_mean = np.where(counts > 0, sums.reshape(n_states, n_actions) / np.maximum(counts, 1), 0.0)
    alpha_effective = 1 - (1 - ALPHA) ** counts # n consecutive alpha-steps toward the batch mean
    Q_soft += alpha_effective * (batch_mean - Q_soft)

a_soft = Q_soft.argmax(axis=1)
pi_soft_greedy = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
pi_soft_greedy[np.arange(n_states), a_soft] = 1.0

print(f"constant-alpha eps-greedy: value gap of greedy policy to v* = "
      f"{np.abs(evaluate_policy(pi_soft_greedy, 1.0) - v_star).max():.4f}")

show_policy(a_soft, "\ngreedy actions of the learned eps-soft policy:")

v_soft = evaluate_policy(eps_greedy(Q_soft, EPS), 1.0)
print(f"\nthe eps-soft policy itself is a little worse than v_* (the price of exploring):"
      f"\n  v(s=6): eps-soft {v_soft[6]:.2f} vs v* {v_star[6]:.2f}")

An episode contributes \(\rho G \ne 0\) only if every choice was left. Any right makes \(\pi(A|S)=0\), and it also makes \(G=0\). Each visit to \(s\) continues with probability \(0.5 \times 0.9 = 0.45\), so the number of visits \(V\) is geometric, and the episode ends in the all-left-and-score way with probability \(0.05/0.55\) given it stops. Such an episode has \(G=1\) and \(\rho = 2^V\).
This implies that the expectation converges
\[
\mathbb E[\rho G] = \sum_{V\ge1} 0.45^{V-1}(0.05)\,2^V = \sum_{V\ge1} 0.1\cdot 0.9^{V-1} = 1
\]
However, the variance does not
\[
\mathbb E[(\rho G)^2] = \sum_{V\ge1} 0.2\cdot 1.8^{V-1} = \infty
\]
So the sample average keeps taking hits of size \(2^V\) and never settles. Weighted IS, in contrast, is exactly 1 here after the first matching episode because every nonzero-weight return is 1.

n_draws_sym = pt.iscalar("n_draws")
rng_infinite = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=7, name="rng_infinite")
rng_after_visits, n_visits = rng_infinite.geometric(p=0.55, size=(n_draws_sym,))
rng_infinite_final, u = rng_after_visits.uniform(size=(n_draws_sym,))
rho_times_G_draw = pt.switch(u < 0.05 / 0.55, 2.0 ** n_visits, 0.0)   # rho * G per episode
infinite_variance_draws = pytensor.function(
    [n_draws_sym],
    rho_times_G_draw,
    updates={rng_infinite: rng_infinite_final}
)

Below we run five independent runs of a million episodes each, plotted as running sample averages. The jumps are single episodes with a large \(2^V\); a curve that has just been hit looks converged for a while, until the next hit resets it.

    running_means.append(running_mean)

Incremental Implementation
Storing every return to re-average is wasteful. Sample means update incrementally, \(V_{n+1} = V_n + \frac1n (G_n - V_n)\), and weighted IS has an equally clean episode-by-episode form. With weights \(W_n = \rho_{t:T-1}\) and cumulative weight \(C_n = \sum_{k=1}^n W_k\):
\[
V_{n+1} = V_n + \frac{W_n}{C_n}\big[G_n - V_n\big], \qquad C_n = C_{n-1} + W_n .
\]
We implement the recursion as a scan over the per-episode \((G, W)\) pairs for state 6 from the previous simulation and check it reproduces the batch weighted-IS estimate exactly.

# per-episode first-visit (G, W) pairs for state 6, in episode order
visits_state6 = first_visits_is & (S_is == 6)
episode_has_state6 = visits_state6.any(axis=0)
t_first_visit = visits_state6.argmax(axis=0)[episode_has_state6]
episodes_with_state6 = np.flatnonzero(episode_has_state6)
G_state6_episodes = G_is[t_first_visit, episodes_with_state6]
W_state6_episodes = rho_is[t_first_visit, episodes_with_state6]

G_episodes_sym, W_episodes_sym = pt.dvector("G_episodes"), pt.dvector("W_episodes")

One step consumes an episode’s \((G, W)\), grows the cumulative weight \(C\), and moves \(V\) a fraction \(W/C\) of the way toward \(G\). Episodes whose weight is zero leave both untouched, which is what the switch guards. A scan over the sequence returns the whole trace of estimates, not just the last one.

def incremental_step(G, W, V_prev, C_prev):
    C_new = C_prev + W
    safe_C = pt.switch(pt.gt(C_new, 0), C_new, 1.0)
    V_new = pt.switch(pt.gt(C_new, 0), V_prev + (W / safe_C) * (G - V_prev), V_prev)
    return V_new, C_new

V_trace, C_trace = pytensor.scan(
    fn=incremental_step,
    sequences=[G_episodes_sym, W_episodes_sym],
    outputs_info=[pt.constant(0.0, dtype="float64"), pt.constant(0.0, dtype="float64")],
    return_updates=False,
)
incremental_fn = pytensor.function([G_episodes_sym, W_episodes_sym], [V_trace, C_trace])

The incremental estimate after the last episode against the batch formula \(\sum W G / \sum W\) agree to floating-point noise because the recursion is an exact rewrite.

V_incremental, C_incremental = incremental_fn(G_state6_episodes, W_state6_episodes)
V_batch = (W_state6_episodes * G_state6_episodes).sum() / W_state6_episodes.sum()

print(f"episodes touching state 6: {G_state6_episodes.size}")
print(f"incremental final estimate: {V_incremental[-1]:.6f}")
print(f"batch weighted-IS estimate: {V_batch:.6f}")
print(f"exact v_pi(6) = {v_target[6]:.3f}")
